 Order

This revision under Section 397 read with Section 401 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 is filed questioning the correctness, legality and proprietary of the order dated 30.05.2023 of the Judicial Magistrate of First Class-I, Cherthala.

entities.text: Judicial Magistrate of First Class-I, Cherthala
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: As per that order, the learned Magistrate dismissed CMP 3530 of 2021 filed by the petitioner for getting signature on the reverse of the fixed deposit receipt examined by a handwriting expert.
That petition was dismissed.
2. Heard the learned counsel for the petitioner, the learned Public Prosecutor and the learned counsel for the 2nd respondent.

3. The case of the petitioner is that at the time when he submitted his papers relating to a tender launched by the Kerala Water Authority, he produced three fixed deposit receipts; two for Rs.3,750/- each and the third for Rs.10,000/-.
In fact, he was obliged to submit two F.D.receipts for Rs.3,750/- each alone.
But he inadvertently produced another F.D.receipt for Rs.10,000/-, the number of which is 62326 dated 17.01.2003.
Since the contract fell through, the 1st respondent forfeited the two F.D.receipts, which was the security deposit.
The third receipt for Rs.10,000/- was to be returned, but the 1st respondent in connivance with the 2nd respondent, forged the signature of the petitioner and encashed it.
With such allegations the petitioner had filed a complaint alleging offences punishable under Sections 420, 465, 467 and 471 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC).
The complaint was initially forwarded for investigation to the police.
After investigation, a final report referring the case was submitted.
On protest, the petitioner filed a complaint.
After necessary enquiry, the court below instituted C.C.No.1584 of 2014.
4. After appearance of respondents 1 and 2, who are the accused, evidence under Section 244 of the Code was recorded by the learned Magistrate.
At that stage, the petitioner filed C.M.P.No.3530 of 2021 seeking to send the F.D. receipt in question for examination by a handwriting expert.
He wanted to examine whether the signature in the F.D. receipts purported to be of the petitioner, was a forged one.
The 2nd respondent resisted that application by filing an objection.

It was pointed out S.Suresh vs Krishnakumar on 16 November, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/72014532/
2 that with respect to that incident occurred 14 years before, the petitioner had filed such a petition,
that too at the fag end of the enquiry under Section 244 of the Code.

sentences.text: Further, it was contended that in the nature of the allegations in the complaint, no such report was necessary.
Moreover, asking the accused to furnish specimen signature will amount to testimonial compulsion.

5. After hearing both sides, the learned Magistrate took the view that there was inordinate delay in filing such a petition and that it was quite impermissible at such a late stage to examine whether the disputed signature was put by the complainant or the 2 nd respondent.
Those findings which lead to the dismissal of the petition are challenged by the petitioner in this revision petition.
6. The petitioner submitted F.D. receipts along with his tender documents in relation to a work tendered by the Kerala Water Authority.
The 1st respondent was the Executive Engineer and the 2nd respondent was the Manager of the Bank, where the F.D. receipts were encashed.
The case of the petitioner is that he was obliged to submit only two F.D. Receipts, each for Rs.3,750/-, whereas by mistake he happened to submit a third F.D. receipt for Rs.10,000/- also.
The allegations against respondents 1 and 2 are that the said F.D. receipt for Rs.10,000/- was encashed by forging the petitioner's signature on the overleaf of it.
Although he stamped and signed on the reverse of other two receipts, no such signature was affixed on the third receipt.

It was in the said circumstances, the petitioner alleged commission of the aforementioned offences by respondents 1 and 2.
7.
From the allegations itself, it is evident that the transaction was with respect to a tender and every aspect of the matter is borne by records.
If F.D. receipt for Rs.10,000/- was encahsed, the same would also be borne by records.

Had the petitioner no obligation to submit such an F.D. receipt, on the other hand, the receipt he submitted had been unauthroisedly encashed, the same can certainly be proved by bringing the documents relating to the tender and the records evidencing encashment of the F.D. receipts.
If the encashment was unrelated to the tender conditions, that can well be proved with the help of documents.

8. If the F.D. receipt in question was encashed and money was remitted to the account of the Kerala Water Authority, which was the employer, the question would be whether such an act amounted to an offences as alleged.
Only if the act was done with a fraudulent or mischievous intention, such an act would amount to an offence.
Therefore, the remittance of the amount covered by the F.D. receipt in question, if it was really encashed, is also a relevant fact.

When adduction of evidence in regard to the aforesaid facts is possible, and that is the best evidence to prove the alleged offences, the request of the petitioner to obtain an opinion regarding the signature in the disputed F.D. receipt at this belated stage cannot be entertained.
An opinion regarding the genuineness of a signature is relevant under Section 45 of the Evidence Act, 1872, but such an opinion shall not override the direct evidence.

When it is very much possible for the complainant to adduce direct evidence in regard to his allegations in the complaint, the plea for obtaining an opinion at this belated stage can no way be justified.
I find no illegality, irregularity or impropriety in the order of the learned Magistrate.
Therefore, the Revision Petition is dismissed.
